sentences.text: Panoplosaurus was a quadrupedal dinosaur approximately 5 meters long and weighing 1600 kilograms, though other estimates suggest a length of 5 to 7 meters and a weight of 1.5 to 1.6 tonnes.
Its skull featured a broad, depressed shape that narrowed to a blunt, triangular snout, with bony plates covering the cheeks.

The animal possessed large, paired osteoderms with a low keel that formed bands around the neck, while its scapula and coracoid bones were completely fused with only a slight thickening marking the suture.
A unique feature of its anatomy was a nasal passage that performed two full 360-degree loops in different planes before reaching the olfactory recess.
At 1600 kg, the dinosaur weighed as much as or more than its contemporary predators.
Variability in its teeth implies a less restrictive feeding strategy than a simple soft-food diet, with microwear indicating abundant foliage and occasional fruit.
Lawrence Lambe discovered the animal in 1917 and formally named the genus Panoplosaurus in 1919, deriving the name from the Greek word for "well-armoured lizard".
Charles M. Sternberg found the first fossil in 1917 at Quarry 69 of the Belly River Group, 210 feet above sea level, or alternatively at Quarry 8 near Little Sandhill Creek.

The holotype specimen CMN 2759 includes a nearly complete skull, most cervical and front dorsal vertebrae with armor, a majority of the forelimb with three articulated fingers, pelvic fragments, foot bones, and hundreds of osteoderms.
Sternberg later identified the ilium support structure in 1921, proposing six vertebrae including four true sacrals.
It is uncertain whether Panoplosaurus possessed gastroliths, as they were not identified in the original specimen material.
Researchers debate whether the unique short snout of the holotype is due to age or sex differences rather than species-specific traits.
Sternberg classified Panoplosaurus within the family Ankylosauridae in 1921, while the genus Edmontonia was described in 1928 as a close relative.

A 1996 analysis by Yuong-Nam Lee nested Panoplosaurus mirus next to Edmontonia, whereas a 2003 analysis by Robert Hill and colleagues identified Panoplosaurus as the sister taxon to a group containing Edmontonia and Animantarx.
Modern phylogenetic analyses place Panoplosaurus in the clade Panoplosaurini, close to Edmontonia and Animantarx, but distinct from Nodosaurus and Struthiosaurus.
Panoplosaurus lived in Alberta, Canada, during the Late Cretaceous period, approximately 79 to 73 million years ago in the Campanian stage, in what is now North America.
All known specimens come from the middle Campanian age of the Dinosaur Park Formation, dating to roughly 76 to 75 million years ago.

The animal inhabited a landscape resembling the swampy coastal plains of modern-day Carolina, where river channels could exceed 200 meters in width and flowed east toward the Bearpaw Sea over ground covered with mosses, lichens, fungi, and decaying plant matter.

It is debated whether Panoplosaurus and Edmontonia are the same taxon, which has complicated interpretations of their distribution and phylogeny, with researchers disagreeing on whether certain specimens, such as ROM 1215, belong to Panoplosaurus or Edmontonia.
Carpenter questioned Sternberg's 1990 identification of four sacrals in Panoplosaurus, noting Edmontonia has only three, though he could not confirm the first sacral was a dorsosacral.
Phylogenetic analyses have consistently placed Panoplosaurus in a group with Edmontonia, but its exact position relative to other nodosaurids like Animantarx and Texasetes remains debated.
